lecons.html:
This module does not replace certified first aid training.

The question people often ask themselves when faced with an emergency is not “what should I do?” — it is “do I have the right to step in, since I’m not a doctor?” And that question paralyzes more people than ignorance itself.

The answer is simple. Yes. You not only have the right, you have a moral obligation to act — within the limits of what you know how to do. A taxi driver who holds an accident victim’s head in the right alignment while waiting for the firefighters may prevent lifelong paralysis. A mother who removes food stuck in her child’s throat in less than thirty seconds may prevent a cardiac arrest. Nobody needs a white coat for that.

This module is not here to turn you into nurses. It is here so that you are not standing there, arms hanging, at the moment someone needs you to do something.

This module has three parts. Each has a specific goal. The first: understand the logic of intervention and master the most common emergencies. The second: recognize silent emergencies, the ones we miss because we don’t know how to read them. The third: anchor all of this in real reflexes, through mental practice.

The fundamental principle: assess before you act

The first reflex of an untrained person facing an emergency is to run toward the victim. It is human. It is also, sometimes, dangerous.

Before touching anyone, there are two questions to ask yourself, in this order.

Step 1 — Is the scene safe for me?

A car accident on a busy road. A burning building. A fallen electrical cable on the ground. If you rush in and become a victim yourself, you double the problem without solving the first one. Look around you. Ten seconds. That is all it takes.

If the scene is not safe, stay at a distance, call for help immediately, and guide people to move away. That is already a lot.

Step 2 — What condition is the victim in?

Two things to check quickly: is the person conscious? Are they breathing? To check consciousness, speak to them loudly — “Can you hear me?” — while touching their shoulder. If they do not respond, check breathing by watching whether the chest rises, for ten seconds at most.

These two answers will decide everything that follows.

Many people call for help and lose precious time because they don’t know what to say. The dispatcher who answers needs information in a precise order. Here is that order.

  1. Your exact location — not “near the market,” but the full address, the neighborhood, a visible landmark. If you are in an area without a clear address, describe it: “I’m on the Porto-Novo road, after the Godomey bridge, on the right-hand side heading toward Calavi.”
  2. What happened — one sentence is enough: accident, unconscious person, child choking, man having convulsions.
  3. How many people are involved.
  4. The apparent condition of the victim — conscious or not, breathing or not, bleeding heavily or not.
  5. Your phone number — in case the call drops, they will call you back.

Do not hang up until you are told to. The dispatcher can guide you in real time while help is on the way.

Emergency numbers in Benin

All these numbers are free from any carrier, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

Practical tip: save these numbers in your phone now, before you need them. And print the list — if your phone is dead or broken in an accident, the paper remains.

This is the most common emergency at family meals, in restaurants, at ceremonies. A piece of meat, a fish bone, a candy. The victim puts their hands to their throat, cannot speak, cannot cough, and their face starts turning red, then blue.

You have between two and five minutes before the brain starts to suffer from lack of oxygen. There is no time to lose.

The Heimlich maneuver

Step 1 — Stand behind the victim.

Step 2 — Wrap both arms around their waist.

Step 3 — Make a fist with your dominant hand. Thumb tucked inward. Place it between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, slightly above the navel.

Step 4 — Cover that fist with your other hand.

Step 5 — Give quick thrusts, inward and upward. Sharp. Powerful. Repeat until the object is expelled or the victim loses consciousness.

Warning: If the victim loses consciousness, gently lay them on the ground and begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Call 112 if you haven’t already.

For an infant under 1 year old

The Heimlich maneuver does not apply. The technique is different: five back blows (between the shoulder blades, with the heel of the hand, baby’s head facing down), alternated with five chest compressions with two fingers in the center of the chest. Repeat until the object is expelled or the baby loses consciousness.

Scenario — choking in a restaurant: The person at the next table suddenly stands up, puts their hands to their throat, cannot speak. They are not coughing. What do you do first? You ask loudly, looking at them: “Are you choking?” — if they nod or cannot answer, you immediately position yourself behind them and begin the Heimlich maneuver. You do not wait. You do not look for your phone first.

Severe bleeding is heavy bleeding that does not stop on its own. The rule is simple and it never changes: press, hold, do not let go.

What to do

  1. Put on gloves if you have them. If not, use a clean plastic bag, a thick cloth, anything between your skin and the blood — disease transmission through blood contact is real.
  2. Place a clean compress or a thick cloth directly on the wound.
  3. Press firmly with your whole palm. Not with your fingertips.
  4. If the blood soaks through, place another compress on top without removing the first one. Keep up the pressure without lifting the compress.
  5. Raise the injured limb above the level of the heart if it is an arm or a leg.
  6. Call 112 or ask someone to call while you keep up the pressure.

Warning: Do not remove an object embedded in the body. A blade, a shard of glass, anything stuck in the flesh must stay in place until help arrives. Removing it can make the bleeding worse.

The improvised tourniquet

A tourniquet is used only as a last resort, when direct pressure is not enough and the bleeding is massive — a severed limb, a cut artery. Use a belt, a rolled cloth, a strap — tighten above the wound (on the heart side), hard enough to stop the bleeding. Note the time. Do not loosen it until help arrives.

The first reflex when faced with a burn must be cool running water. Not ice-cold — cold like tap water. For at least fifteen to twenty minutes.

Cool running water for 15 to 20 minutes. That is all you do in the first minutes. Nothing else.

What you do not do — ever: no butter, no oil, no toothpaste, no egg white, no plant leaves. These common remedies trap heat in the burn instead of dissipating it, and can cause serious infections.

After cooling: cover the burn with clean plastic wrap or a very clean cloth. Do not pop blisters. See a doctor for any burn larger than the palm of the hand, or any burn on the face, hands, feet, or genitals.

Scenario — boiling oil: Someone spills a pan of boiling oil on their forearm. The first reflex: take them to the tap and put the forearm under cool running water. No ice water, no ice cubes. For twenty minutes. Meanwhile, help them stay calm and call a doctor or 136 to assess the severity.

Silent emergencies are the ones we miss — not for lack of courage, but for lack of reading. A cardiac arrest can look like someone sleeping. A stroke can look like someone drunk. A seizure can panic all the witnesses to the point that nobody really helps. This chapter is here for that: learning to read what you see.

Stroke — a cerebrovascular accident

A stroke is a sudden interruption of blood flow in part of the brain. Every minute counts — literally. For every minute without treatment, two million neurons die. The lasting damage depends largely on how quickly medical help arrives.

The problem is that a stroke is subtle at first. The person may simply seem tired, or confused, or to have had too much to drink. The recognition tool is called FAST.

The FAST test

  • Ask the person to smile. Does one side of the face stay still or droop? F as in Face.
  • Ask them to raise both arms at the same time. Does one fall or drift down? A as in Arms.
  • Ask them to say a simple sentence: “The weather is nice today.” Is the speech slurred, incomprehensible, or do they have difficulty finding words? S as in Speech.
  • If even one of these three signs is present, call 112 immediately. T as in Time to call.

Warning: Do not give anything to drink or eat. Do not let the person drive. Do not tell them to “wait for it to pass.” A stroke does not pass on its own.

Lay the person down, head slightly raised. Cover them if they are shivering. Speak to them calmly. Wait for help without moving them.

Scenario — stroke in a relative: Your uncle, during Sunday lunch, drops his fork. He tries to speak but the words don’t come out right. His smile is lopsided. You do the FAST test: asymmetrical face — yes. Arms: the left one drops — yes. Slurred speech — yes. You call 112 immediately, you tell him not to move, you lay him down slightly. You do not give him water. You do not tell him it will pass.

Cardiac arrest is the moment when the heart stops pumping blood. The brain can survive four to six minutes without oxygen. After that, the damage becomes irreversible. CPR does not replace the heart — it keeps things going while waiting for help. It can double or triple the chances of survival.

How to recognize a cardiac arrest

  • The person is unconscious and does not respond to voice or touch.
  • They are not breathing, or they have agonal breathing — loud, irregular gasps that do not look like normal breathing.
  • Their face may be gray or bluish.

CPR — how to do it

Here is CPR explained step by step, so that you can picture each movement.

Step 1 — Lay the victim on their back, on a hard surface.

Step 2 — Call 112 or ask someone to do it while you begin.

Step 3 — Position your hands. Interlock your fingers. Place the heel of your dominant hand in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone. Only the heel — not the fingers, not the whole palm.

Step 4 — Arms straight, vertically above the chest. Your weight, not your strength. You use your whole body.

Step 5 — Compressions. Push the chest down five to six centimeters. Fast — one hundred to one hundred twenty compressions per minute, about two per second. Let the chest rise back up completely between compressions.

Step 6 — Continue without stopping until help arrives or until the victim starts breathing normally again.

The rhythm of the compressions: the Bee Gees’ song “Stayin’ Alive” is at exactly one hundred and three beats per minute. If you know that rhythm, sing it in your head during the compressions. It may seem out of place — it works.

Warning: CPR can break ribs. That is unpleasant to know, but it is not a reason to stop. A broken rib heals. A brain deprived of oxygen for too long does not.

A seizure — an epileptic fit — is frightening to watch. The person falls, their body stiffens and then shakes violently, they may lose control of their bladder, their eyes may roll back. It is impressive. And that is precisely why the people around panic and sometimes do exactly what should not be done.

What to do

  1. Put something soft underneath — a folded piece of clothing, your hand. Do not restrain them. Protect the head.
  2. Move away any hard or sharp objects within reach.
  3. Note the time the seizure started.
  4. After the seizure, place the person in the recovery position (see below).
  5. Call 112 if the seizure lasts more than five minutes, if it is the person’s first seizure, or if they do not regain consciousness after the seizure.

What you do not do — ever: do not put anything in the person’s mouth. Not a spoon, not your fingers, not a cloth. People often say you must “stop the person from biting their tongue” — that is false. You cannot swallow your tongue. But you can break the person’s teeth, or lose your own fingers.

Someone who suddenly becomes shaky, confused, pale, sweats for no reason, and answers incoherently — may be having hypoglycemia. Their blood sugar level has dropped too low.

What to do if the person is conscious

Give them fast sugar immediately: a glass of sweetened fruit juice, a soda, sugar cubes, honey. No dark chocolate, no plain water. Wait fifteen minutes. If there is no improvement, call 112.

Warning: If the person is unconscious, do not give anything to drink or eat. Place them in the recovery position and call 112 immediately.

Drowning

In case of drowning, the first rule is the one most often forgotten: do not enter the water if you are not a confident swimmer. A panicking drowning person can drown their rescuer. First look for an alternative: a rope, a buoy, a knotted piece of clothing, a plank.

Once the victim is out of the water, check consciousness and breathing. If they are unconscious and not breathing: start CPR immediately. Five mouth-to-mouth rescue breaths to begin with (if you know how), then thirty compressions, then two breaths — repeat. Call 112.

The recovery position is used for any unconscious person who is still breathing. It prevents the person from choking on their own vomit or saliva.

Step 1 — Kneel beside the victim, who is lying on their back.

Step 2 — Place the arm closest to you at a right angle, elbow bent, palm facing up.

Step 3 — Bring the other arm across the chest. Palm against the cheek on the side away from you.

Step 4 — Bend the knee of the leg farthest from you.

Step 5 — Roll the victim toward you by pulling on the bent knee. They end up on their side.

Step 6 — Adjust the hand under the cheek to keep the head slightly tilted back. This keeps the airway open.

Step 7 — Check breathing regularly while waiting for help.

Scenario — silent emergency: You find your neighbor lying in her yard, unconscious. You speak to her loudly and touch her shoulder — no reaction. You look at her chest: she is breathing, slowly. You see no visible injury. You call 112 immediately, you tilt her head slightly back to clear the airway, you place her in the recovery position, and you wait for help beside her, checking her breathing every two minutes.

This last part does not present new content. It does something else: it turns what you have learned into reflexes. Because in a real emergency, you won’t have time to recall a list. You will need the right action to come on its own.

Guided mental simulation is recognized by first aid trainers as an effective tool for building reflexes without a mannequin. That is what we offer you here: scenarios, one by one. Read the situation. Say out loud — or in your head — what you do first, second, third.

No pressure. No competition. The goal is that the next time you find yourself in one of these situations, your body already knows what to do.

lecons.titre: General rules, basic kit, and conclusion
lecons.html:
General rules to remember

These rules apply in almost every emergency. Memorize them.

  • Assess the scene before stepping in. Your safety comes first.
  • Call 112 early, not at the end. The dispatcher can guide you in real time.
  • Be precise about your location. It is the most important thing you will say.
  • Do not move a victim unless they are in immediate danger (fire, drowning, imminent collapse).
  • Do not give anything to drink or eat to someone who is unconscious or convulsing.
  • Do not remove an object embedded in the body.
  • Keep pressure on a bleeding wound and never release it to look.
  • Continue CPR without interruption until help arrives. Fatigue is normal. If there are several of you, take turns every two minutes.

The basic kit, available locally

Here is what it is reasonable to have at home or in your bag. These are items you can find in any pharmacy in Benin, at a moderate cost.

ItemWhat it is for
Disposable gloves (latex or vinyl)Handling a victim without risk of contamination
Sterile compressesPressing on a wound, cleaning
Gauze bandageHolding a dressing in place
Medical adhesive tapeSecuring a dressing
Antiseptic solution (Betadine or Dakin’s)Cleaning a wound before dressing it
Blunt-tipped scissorsCutting clothing or bandages
ThermometerChecking a fever
Emergency blanket (if possible)Protecting against thermal shock
Printed list of emergency numbersAvailable even without network or battery
Basic personal medicationsParacetamol, antihistamine

One more tip: talk about this kit with your family. Every adult in the household must know where it is. A hidden kit that nobody knows about is useless in an emergency.

Closing words of the module

First aid does not require heroism. It requires presence of mind and a few skills learned in advance.

Most people who do not step in during an emergency are not afraid of death. They are afraid of doing it wrong. Yet an imperfect action is almost always better than no action. The brain of an adult in cardiac arrest begins to suffer after four minutes. You have four minutes to decide whether to act or not.

What you have learned in these three parts — recognize, call, act — is exactly what it takes to make good use of those four minutes. Not more. But not less either.

The real test is not the end of this module. It is the day when, in a restaurant, in a street, in your own living room, someone will need you not to be paralyzed. On that day, what you learned here will be there.

objectifs: ✦  You know you have the right, and the moral obligation, to act within the limits of what you know how to do.
✦  You assess the scene before stepping in: your safety first, then the victim’s condition.
✦  You know how to call for help by giving the right information, in the right order.
✦  You know how to act in the face of choking, severe bleeding, and a burn.
✦  You recognize a stroke, a cardiac arrest, a seizure, a diabetic emergency, and a drowning, and you know what to do.
✦  You know how to place an unconscious person who is breathing in the recovery position.
✦  You have a basic kit and the list of emergency numbers at home, and your family knows where they are.

qcm.q: When facing an emergency, what is the very first question to ask yourself before touching the victim?
c: Do I have the right to step in without being a doctor?
Is the scene safe for me?
Do I know the victim?
Has someone else already called?
qcm.e: If you become a victim yourself, you double the problem without solving the first one. Look around for ten seconds. If the scene is not safe: stay at a distance, call for help, and guide people to move away.

qcm.q: When you call for help, what information do you give first?
c: Your exact location: full address, neighborhood, visible landmark
Your phone number
Your first name and your occupation
The number of people involved
qcm.e: The order: exact location, what happened, how many people, the victim’s apparent condition, your phone number. Do not hang up until you are told to: the dispatcher can guide you in real time.

qcm.q: What number do you call in Benin for a life-threatening medical emergency (SAMU)?
c: 112, free, 24/7, from all carriers
qcm.e: 118 is the firefighters’ number and 117 is the police. All are free, 24/7.

qcm.q: An adult is choking and can neither speak nor cough. Where do you place your fist for the Heimlich maneuver?
c: On the upper abdomen, flat, with gentle movements
On the back, between the shoulder blades, with the heel of the hand only
Between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, slightly above the navel, with inward and upward thrusts
In the middle of the chest, with downward compressions
qcm.e: You stand behind the victim, wrap your arms around their waist, cover your fist with your other hand, and give sharp thrusts, until the object is expelled or they lose consciousness. For an infant under one year old, the technique is different: back blows and two-finger chest compressions.

qcm.q: A wound is bleeding heavily and the compress is already soaked through. What do you do?
c: I lift the compress to see whether the bleeding continues
I place another compress on top, without removing the first one, and I keep up the pressure
I remove the compress and put on a clean one
I loosen it a little so the blood can circulate
qcm.e: Press, hold, do not let go. If an object is embedded in the body, you do not remove it: it stays in place until help arrives.

qcm.q: When do you use an improvised tourniquet?
c: As a last resort, when direct pressure is not enough and the bleeding is massive: you tighten above the wound, you note the time, and you do not loosen it
Only after removing the object embedded in the wound
As soon as a wound bleeds a little
Never: it is always forbidden
qcm.e: The basic rule remains: press, hold, do not let go.

qcm.q: Someone burned their forearm with boiling oil. What is the first action?
c: Put the forearm under cool running water, 15 to 20 minutes minimum
Pop the blisters to drain the fluid
Put ice cubes on the burn
Apply butter or oil to ease the pain
qcm.e: Cool running water, not ice-cold. Never butter, oil, toothpaste, egg white, or plants: they trap the heat and can cause serious infections. Then, clean plastic wrap or a very clean cloth, and a doctor for any burn larger than the palm or on the face, hands, feet, or genitals.

qcm.q: FAST test: how many signs are needed to call 112 immediately?
c: None, as long as the person stays conscious
At least two
Just one is enough
All three at the same time
qcm.e: F: the face (one side droops when they smile). A: the arms (one falls when they raise both). S: speech trouble. T: time to call, you call. You give nothing to drink or eat, you do not let the person drive, you do not say “wait for it to pass.”

qcm.q: Your uncle drops his fork, his face droops on one side, and his speech becomes slurred. What do you do?
c: I give him sugar water and wait for it to pass
I call 112 right away, I lay him down with his head slightly raised, and I give him nothing to drink or eat
I shake him to wake him up
I let him drive himself to the hospital
qcm.e: Just one sign of the FAST test is enough. A stroke does not pass on its own.

qcm.q: An adult is unconscious and not breathing. How do you do the CPR compressions?
c: On the left side of the chest, 2 cm deep
With the fingertips, gently, about 1 per second
With the palm on the belly, 5 to 6 cm deep
Heel of one hand in the center of the chest, arms straight, 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute
qcm.e: You lay the victim on their back, on a hard surface, you call 112 (or ask someone to do it), and you let the chest rise back up between each compression. You continue until help arrives. A broken rib heals, a brain deprived of oxygen does not.

qcm.q: A child is having a seizure. What do you absolutely not do?
c: Place them in the recovery position after the seizure
Note the time the seizure started
Put something in their mouth so they don’t bite their tongue
Protect their head with something soft
qcm.e: You cannot swallow your tongue. On the other hand, you can break the person’s teeth or lose your own fingers. You call 112 if the seizure lasts more than five minutes, if it is the first seizure, or if the person does not regain consciousness.

qcm.q: A conscious person becomes shaky, pale, confused, and sweats for no reason (hypoglycemia). What do you give them?
c: Nothing at all, we wait for help
Fast sugar: sweetened fruit juice, soda, sugar cubes, or honey
Dark chocolate
Plain water
qcm.e: You wait fifteen minutes: if there is no improvement, you call 112. If the person is unconscious, you give nothing to drink or eat, you place them in the recovery position, and you call 112 right away.

qcm.q: A child is drowning in a river and you are a poor swimmer. What do you do first?
c: I stay still and wait for them to come up
I wait to see whether they can swim
I go into the water right away: every second counts
I look for an alternative: rope, buoy, knotted clothing, plank, and I call 112
qcm.e: A panicking drowning person can drown their rescuer. Once the victim is out of the water, you check consciousness and breathing. If they are unconscious and not breathing: CPR (five rescue breaths to begin with if you know how, then thirty compressions and two breaths) and call 112.

qcm.q: Who is the recovery position used for?
c: Any injured person, as a rule
A person who is choking and can still cough
An unconscious person who is still breathing
A person in cardiac arrest
qcm.e: The recovery position prevents the person from choking on their vomit or saliva. You keep checking their breathing regularly while waiting for help. If they are not breathing, it is no longer the recovery position: it is CPR.

qcm.q: Which general rule applies in almost every emergency?
c: Call 112 early, be precise about your location, and move the victim only if they are in immediate danger
Give the victim something to drink to calm them down
Quickly move any victim to make them comfortable
Call 112 at the end, when everything else has been tried
qcm.e: The dispatcher can guide you in real time. Do not move a victim except in immediate danger (fire, drowning, imminent collapse). An imperfect action is almost always better than no action.

exercices.titre: Emergency numbers: which one to call?
exercices.consigne: Five situations: choose the right number. After each choice, you see the expected answer. Then save the list in your phone and on paper.

champs.label: A person is unconscious and not breathing. Which number do you dial?
champs.explication: 112 is the number for life-threatening medical emergencies: free, 24 hours a day, from all carriers.

champs.label: A house is on fire. Which number do you dial?
champs.explication: 118 is the number of the firefighters (ABPC), free, 24 hours a day.

champs.label: You want to report an assault in the street. Which number do you dial?
champs.explication: 117 (and 116 as an alternative) is the number of the Republican Police.

champs.label: A child has a minor burn and you want a health professional to assess how serious it is. Which number can you call?
champs.explication: 136 provides health information. The manual also cites it for assessing the severity of a burn.

champs.label: An emergency involves a child in danger. Which number is provided for these emergencies?
champs.explication: 160 is the number of the Juvenile Brigade, for emergencies involving children.

champs.label: I have saved these numbers in my phone (SAMU 112, firefighters 118, police 117, health 136, toll-free 166, juvenile brigade 160).
I wrote the list on paper and put it in a place everyone at home knows: if my phone is dead or broken, the paper remains.

exercices.consigne: Read each situation and say out loud, or in your head, what you do first, second, third. Then choose your answer and compare it with the expected one. No pressure, no competition: the goal is for your body to already know what to do. Reread the relevant lessons if needed.

champs.label: Scenario 1: at the restaurant. A fifty-year-old man at the next table half rises, puts both hands to his throat, and turns red. He is not coughing and not shouting. What do you do?
options: I ask loudly whether he is choking; if he nods or cannot answer, I stand behind him and begin the Heimlich maneuver, asking someone to call 112
I first look for my phone to call 112
I give him water to drink
I lay him on the ground and begin chest compressions
champs.bonne: I ask loudly whether he is choking; if he nods or cannot answer, I stand behind him and begin the Heimlich maneuver, asking someone to call 112
champs.explication: You do not waste time looking for your phone: you act, and someone else calls. CPR only begins if he loses consciousness.

champs.label: Scenario 2: in the street. Someone in front of you collapses on the sidewalk. They do not respond to voice or touch, and their chest is not rising. What do you do?
options: I place them in the recovery position and wait
I shout to get attention and ask someone to call 112, I check breathing (ten seconds) and I start CPR right away, without stopping until help arrives
I slap them to wake them up for several minutes
I walk away: I’m not a doctor
champs.bonne: I shout to get attention and ask someone to call 112, I check breathing (ten seconds) and I start CPR right away, without stopping until help arrives
champs.explication: Hands in the center of the chest, arms straight, deep and fast compressions. The recovery position is reserved for an unconscious person who is breathing. And you have the right, and even the moral obligation, to act.

champs.label: Scenario 3: at home. A seven-year-old child in the yard is shaking violently: arms and legs out of control, eyes rolled back, foam at the mouth. What do you do?
options: I put a spoon in their mouth so they don’t bite their tongue
I hold them firmly to stop the shaking
I protect their head with something soft, I move hard objects away, I note the time, I put nothing in their mouth, and after the seizure I place them in the recovery position
I pour water on their face
champs.bonne: I protect their head with something soft, I move hard objects away, I note the time, I put nothing in their mouth, and after the seizure I place them in the recovery position
champs.explication: You call 112 if the seizure lasts more than five minutes or if it is the first time, then you wait for help.

champs.label: Scenario 4: family gathering. Your 68-year-old grandmother complains of pain in her left arm, she is pale and sweating. Two minutes later, she loses consciousness. What do you do?
options: I sit her in an armchair and give her sugar water
I make her walk a little so she relaxes
I let it go: she has felt faint before
I call 112 immediately, I check consciousness and breathing, and if she is not breathing I start CPR; I give her nothing to drink
champs.bonne: I call 112 immediately, I check consciousness and breathing, and if she is not breathing I start CPR; I give her nothing to drink
champs.explication: Pain in the left arm and sweating often precede a heart attack: it is a suspected cardiac arrest.

champs.label: Scenario 5: a four-year-old child grabs a pot of hot water. The water spills onto their arm and shoulder: red skin, blisters starting to form. What do you do first?
options: I apply butter or oil to ease the pain
I put ice cubes on the burn
I put the arm under cool running water (not ice-cold), 15 to 20 minutes minimum, then I cover it with clean plastic wrap and I call a doctor or 136
champs.bonne: I put the arm under cool running water (not ice-cold), 15 to 20 minutes minimum, then I cover it with clean plastic wrap and I call a doctor or 136
champs.explication: No butter, no oil, no toothpaste, no plants. You remove the clothing around the burn if possible, unless it is stuck.

champs.label: Scenario 6: at the market, a woman suddenly becomes shaky, pale, confused, and sweaty. She is conscious and says she is diabetic. What do you do?
options: I give her a glass of sweetened fruit juice (or sugar, honey), I wait fifteen minutes, and I call 112 if it does not improve
I give her plain water and invite her to rest
I do nothing: we must wait for help
champs.bonne: I give her a glass of sweetened fruit juice (or sugar, honey), I wait fifteen minutes, and I call 112 if it does not improve
champs.explication: No plain water, no dark chocolate. If she loses consciousness, you give nothing more to drink: recovery position and 112 immediately.

champs.label: Scenario 7: a child falls into a river and does not come back to the surface. You are a poor swimmer. What do you do?
options: I dive in to get them out, there is no time to lose
I look for a rope, a buoy, a knotted piece of clothing, or a plank to hold out to them, and I ask someone to call 112
I wait for them to come up on their own
I go home to look for help
champs.bonne: I look for a rope, a buoy, a knotted piece of clothing, or a plank to hold out to them, and I ask someone to call 112
champs.explication: Do not enter the water if you are not a confident swimmer: a panicking drowning person can drown their rescuer. Once the child is out of the water, you check consciousness and breathing, and if needed you start CPR.

champs.label: For each scenario, I said out loud my first three actions, before looking at the answer.

exercices.titre: What you do, what you never do
exercices.consigne: Ten actions: do or never do? After each choice, you see the explanation.

champs.label: 1. Putting a spoon or a cloth in the mouth of a person having a seizure.
champs.explication: You cannot swallow your tongue, and you risk breaking the person’s teeth or losing your fingers.

champs.label: 2. Putting butter, oil, or toothpaste on a burn.
champs.explication: These remedies trap heat in the burn and can cause serious infections. Only cool running water, 15 to 20 minutes.

champs.label: 3. Removing a blade or a shard of glass embedded in the body.
champs.explication: The object stays in place until help arrives: removing it can make the bleeding worse.

champs.label: 4. Keeping pressure on a bleeding wound without ever releasing it to look.
champs.explication: Press, hold, do not let go. If the compress is soaked through, you place another on top without removing the first.

champs.label: 5. Giving something to drink to a person who may be having a stroke.
champs.explication: You give nothing to drink or eat, you do not let the person drive, and you do not tell them to wait for it to pass.

champs.label: 6. Continuing CPR even if a rib cracks.
champs.explication: A broken rib heals. A brain deprived of oxygen for too long does not.

champs.label: 7. Jumping into the water to save a drowning person when you are a poor swimmer.
champs.explication: You first look for an alternative: rope, buoy, knotted clothing, plank.

champs.label: 8. Calling 112 early, at the start of the emergency.
champs.explication: The dispatcher can guide you in real time while help is on the way.

champs.label: 9. Giving a glass of sweetened fruit juice to a conscious person with low blood sugar.
champs.explication: Fast sugar, then you wait fifteen minutes. If there is no improvement: 112.

champs.label: 10. Moving an accident victim so they are more comfortable.
champs.explication: You do not move a victim except in immediate danger: fire, drowning, imminent collapse.

exercices.consigne: Prepare your call in advance, because in an emergency you won’t have time to search for words. Reread the lesson “Calling for help.”

champs.label: My location, as I would tell it to the dispatcher from my home: the full address or, failing that, the neighborhood and a visible landmark (not “near the market”)

My complete call for this situation: my 5-year-old nephew is choking on a piece of food and can no longer breathe. Write, in order, everything you say (location, what happened, how many people, the victim’s condition, your number)
When can I hang up?

exercices.consigne: Take inventory of the basic kit from the lesson on general rules. These are items you can find in any pharmacy in Benin, at a moderate cost. A hidden kit that nobody knows about is useless in an emergency.

champs.label: What I already have in my kit or in my bag (check what is there)
What I am missing and how I will get it (pharmacy), or “nothing is missing”
Where is the kit, and who in my household knows where it is? If no one, how will I make sure every adult knows?

exercices.titre: Passing a skill on to someone close to me
exercices.consigne: Choose one skill from this module and explain it to someone around you: spouse, an older child, a neighbor, a colleague. Explaining is the best way to remember, and it is one more person who will know what to do.

champs.label: The skill I choose to explain
options: Severe bleeding: press, hold, do not let go
Seizures: what you do and what you don’t

champs.label: The person I explain it to (first name, relationship to me)
I explained and showed it to them, and I asked them to tell it back to me in their own words.
What they remembered well, what they forgot, and what I understood myself by explaining it
What was holding me back from stepping in before this module (fear of doing it wrong, of not having the right, of not knowing) and what has changed
The emergency numbers I know by heart, and where my list is posted
The skill I master best, and the one I still need to review (and how)
